On 18 September 2026 (KST), a Korean medicine hospital in Busan, South Korea was hit by the NightSpire ransomware group (file extension ".nspire", ransom note "[NSPIRE_MSG].txt").




Timeline:

- ~16 Aug 2026: Attackers gained access to our internal network and installed AnyDesk on our Oracle database (EMR) server for persistent remote access. They remained inside for about one month, most likely exfiltrating patient data.

- 18 Sep 2026, 07:29-07:32 KST (17 Sep 22:29 UTC): Our EMR database server (Oracle datafiles, ~90 GB) and our NAS backup server were both encrypted. All backups were destroyed.

- The ransom note demanded 10% of yearly revenue and threatened to publish stolen patient data on their Tor leak site and to report us to regulators.We negotiated through their Tor chat portal. Initial demand was USD 50,000; final agreed amount was USD 20,000, paid in Bitcoin (0.25 BTC total) to the attacker's wallet in two transactions on 19 Sep 2026.




We are reporting the attacker's Bitcoin address and both transaction IDs so exchanges and investigators can flag and trace these funds. This attack involved theft of medical patient data. We have also reported the incident to Korean authorities (KISA, police, PIPC).

On June 10, 2026, at approximately 15:05 UTC, an automated ransomware attack targeted a MariaDB 11 database server (Docker container) exposed on the internet via port 3307. The attacker, operating from IP address 64.89.163.142 (AS401626 Netiface America / Meowcore Softworks LLC, Frankfurt am Main, Germany), gained access using the default root credential (username: root, password: "root").

The attacker first scanned the port at 02:16 UTC (2 failed login attempts), then returned 13 hours later. After authenticating, the ransomware dropped the existing database named "smallville" and created a new database called "RECOVER_YOUR_DATA" containing a single table with the following ransom note:

"All your data was backed up by us. You must pay 0.0137 bitcoin to bc1qk9kvwhzt60u3eqcjllqlj44h0tj7w7n72apz99 or in 48 hours, your data will be publicly disclosed and deleted."

The attack window was approximately 20 seconds (15:05:57 to 15:05:59 UTC), indicating a fully automated tool. The attacker then issued a SHUTDOWN command to the MariaDB server. The Bitcoin address shows zero transactions, suggesting it was generated fresh for this victim.

The database contained Discord bot operational data (support tickets, user IDs). No evidence of data exfiltration was found. The database was restored from a

backup dated June 5, 2026.

message_preview:
I downloaded the software from bitaddress.org and used the software to create a paper wallet offline. I, then, deleted the software to make sure not to leave any trace or something like this. I sent some low amount of Bitcoin to this address to make sure it works. It worked. Then I sent much more Bitcoin to this address. Unfortunately, despite I have never shared my private key anywhere, my funds have been moved to another unknown address without my permission. I scanned my computer to look if there is any malware or something like that. It found nothing. But I used Wireshark to look for suspicious data transfer. Afterwards, I found some IP addresses relating to Tor exit nodes (svchost.exe connects to tor servers). Then I found out that ep6nmzspno.dll on my computer abused svchost.exe to steal my funds after more scanning with an antivirus software.

It connected Tor nodes around the world. There are many IP addresses I could captured relating this malware activity. This malware in my laptop can be detectable when I copy and paste a Bitcoin address, because they do not match; the virus knows I copied a Bitcoin address and changes it to the scammer's address. This is called keylogger as I searched this. I strongly suspect there is also a clipboard hijacker, because I unfortunately realized that the private and public keys I generated do not match, probably because they were altered by this malware. I know this because when I created a cold wallet using this private key on Binance, It literally gave me a different address with no transaction history. This implies that I actually unknowingly sent my Bitcoins to the scammer's address. The virus also seems to use too much ram, because even if no program is open, my laptop uses more than 10gb of ram, sometimes even 15gb of ram.
